newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says U.S. is economic model for world. [Corrected 22:52 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Clinton says U.S. is economic model for world. [Corrected 22:52 GMT]

text.p: Speaking on the eve of a summit of big industrial nations, President Bill Clinton on Thursday boasted about the soaring U.S. economy and held up the policies driving it as a model for the world.

In a keynote speech before the weekend summit to be attended by Russia and the Group of Seven nations -- the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan -- Clinton said the boom was based on balancing the budget, investing in education and expanding trade.
"We host our partners at a time when America's economy is the healthiest in a generation and the strongest in the world," he said.

Clinton credited "a new American economic approach that required us to puncture myths and push past yesterday's failed debates ...(enabling) us to move earlier and more strongly than most other nations into the new global economy."

According to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the United States will have unemployment of 5.0 percent this year, growth of 3.6 percent and a budget deficit of just 1.1 percent of its gross domestic product.

The economies of France, Germany and Italy, on the other hand, are all sluggish and suffer from double-digit unemployment. All three are forecast by the OECD this year to have 3.2 percent budget-deficit-to-GDP ratios. All remain wedded to expensive, cumbersome social programmes.

Clinton, speaking to a crowd of about 500 people gathered outside a high-tech television facility in this Denver suburb, was especially vocal about the importance of international trade, a controversial issue with some elements of his Democratic Party and conservative Republicans.
"We have chosen to reach out, not to be afraid of competition, to embrace the possibilities of the global economy and to work to make sure it works for ordinary American citizens," Clinton said.

He said the United States, a country with slighly less than five percent (corrects from "one-fifth") of the world population and slightly more than 20 percent of its wealth and income, could not sustain its standard of living unless it sold more to other countries.
"We cannot afford to not keep reaching out to the rest of the world and I intend to do it," the president said.

Clinton, who met later with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, said in his speech the United States and Japan had reached a new agreement on a consultative process to open Japanese markets to U.S. exports like telecommunications. Colorado is a hub of the telecommunications industry.

Aides said Clinton came to the summit with a sense of satisfaction that he was a leader to be envied because of the buoyant U.S. economy rather than, as has often been the case for presidents in the past, as a summit whipping boy.
The White House issued a fact sheet noting the contrast since 1990, when the United States last hosted an economic summit.

"At that time, the economy was in recession, the budget deficit was steadily climbing, more jobs were being destroyed than being created and our G7 partners criticised the U.S. for economic mismanagement," the paper said.
